tasks.task_description: Model the effects of connected, self-driving cars on traffic flow for I-5, I-90, I-405 and SR-520 in Thurston, Pierce, King and Snohomish counties, as a function of the fleet percentage p (10%, 50%, 90%). Answer the Governor's four questions: (1) how do effects change as p increases; (2) do equilibria exist; (3) is there a tipping point where performance changes markedly; (4) under what conditions should lanes be dedicated to the fleet, and what other policy changes are suggested.
tasks.task_analysis: Data preparation: 224 segments, 4 routes (I-5: 135 seg/117.4 mi, I-90: 27 seg/23.4 mi, I-405: 47 seg/30.3 mi, SR-520: 15 seg/12.8 mi), cleaned from 2017_MCM_Problem_C_Data.csv. Repairs: header whitespace stripped, trailing space in the 'Number of Lanes DECR MP direction ' column fixed, mileposts and ADT coerced to numerics, lane counts to integers, route type validated (all IS/SR), 0 duplicates, 0 invalid rows; 201 empty Comments cells left as-is (not used). Corridor profiles are mile-weighted: I-5 ADT 150,330 / 3.53 lanes, I-90 101,108 / 3.02, I-405 144,819 / 2.80, SR-520 75,384 / 2.00. Assumptions: (A1) 2015 ADT is stationary enough to represent a near-term planning day; (A2) the ADT-to-peak-hour conversion uses a peak-hour factor f and a peak-direction share d; (A3) at rush hour the binding constraint is lane capacity (free-flow speed is not binding); (A4) the connected fleet is distributed uniformly over the corridor and mixes into every general lane; (A5) platooning raises per-lane capacity at speed, but the benefit in mixed traffic is discounted by human drivers' dispersion; (A6) demand does not change with p at planning level (no induced demand). Method: a peak-hour, lane-level supply/demand model per segment. It is sound for this problem because the dataset supplies exactly the two inputs such a model needs (traffic volume and lane count per segment) and the decision questions (tipping point, dedicated lanes) are about whether demand meets per-lane capacity, which is a static equilibrium comparison rather than a dynamics question; the full dynamics would only refine where, not whether, congestion occurs.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: p = fleet share in {0.10, 0.50, 0.90}; q_lane = peak-direction lane demand, vphpl; c0 = general-lane practical capacity, vphpl; c_mix(p) = mixed-traffic per-lane capacity; m = fleet-only (platooned) per-lane multiplier; alpha = mixed-traffic uplift coefficient; g_pen = human dispersion penalty; d = peak-direction share of peak-hour volume; f = peak-hour factor; occ = occupancy. Equations (all implemented in code/model.py, run on data/cleaned_data.csv): q_lane(s) = ADT_s * f * d / (100 * lanes_s(dir)); c_mix(p) = c0 * (1 + alpha*p) * (1 - g_pen*p); congestion onset at segment s when q_lane(s) >= c_mix(p); corridor VLOS-like state = count of congested segments; tipping point p*(corridor) = smallest p in [0, 0.95] at which no segment is congested. Dedicated-lane test (high-benefit-over-cost rule): displaced general lane person throughput = min(q_lane0, c0) * occ; dedicated fleet lane person throughput = min(c0*(1 + alpha*p), p * q_lane0) * occ, where q_lane0 = corridor-weighted vphpl at p = 0 and the dedicated lane is demand-limited by the fleet's share of corridor demand; the lane is 'worth it' iff the second >= the first. Parameter table (empirical inputs; every empirical number the model reports is in this table or from the task dataset): f = 0.10, interval [0.08, 0.12], source: expert exchange 1 (peak-hour volume ~8-12% of ADT on these corridors); d = 0.45, interval [0.40, 0.50], source: planning-level peak-direction split for a strongly commuter-anchored corridor (expert exchange 1 established the peak is sharply concentrated; split swept [0.40, 0.50] because the dataset gives no directional data); c0 = 2000 vphpl, interval [1900, 2200], source: expert exchange 1 (peak-direction flow 2000-2400 vphpl at or above practical capacity) consistent with the HCM basic-segment practical capacity for level freeway (TRB, Highway Capacity Manual, basic freeway segment capacity ~2000 pc/h/ln); m = 1.5, interval [1.5, 2.0], source: expert exchange 2 (platooning headways 0.5-1.0 s vs 1.5-2.0 s human; ~1.5-2x vehicles/lane/hour); alpha = 0.5, interval [0.4, 0.7], source: derived so full-share mixed capacity c0*(1+alpha) reaches the low end of the exchange-2 range (swept); g_pen = 0.15, interval [0.10, 0.20], source: residual mixed-traffic dispersion penalty from the non-automated majority (swept); occ = 1.25, interval [1.2, 1.4], source: expert exchange 3 (general-lane person throughput 2400-2800 pax/h at 1.2-1.4 occupancy). Solution procedure: (1) clean data (code/clean_data.py); (2) per-segment q_lane and c_mix for p in {0.10, 0.50, 0.90}; (3) count congested segments per corridor; (4) scan p from 0 to 0.95 in steps of 0.01 for tipping points; (5) run the dedicated-lane test at each p; (6) sweep f, alpha, g_pen, d over the stated intervals (24-combination sweep) to check robustness (logs/run/model.log, logs/run/model_dedicated.log).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (base case f=0.10, d=0.45, c0=2000, alpha=0.50, g_pen=0.15; full sweep in logs/run/model.log). (1) Effects vs p: worst-segment vphpl is fixed by the data — I-5 3630 (the 2-lane I-90-approach segment, milepost 163.36-163.48, ADT 238,000), I-90 2430, I-405 3982, SR-520 2452 — so demand never falls; only supply rises, from c_mix=2068 vphpl at p=0.10 to 2312 at p=0.50 and 2508 at p=0.90. Congested segments (q_lane >= c_mix): I-5 61/135 -> 39/135 -> 24/135; I-90 3/27 -> 1/27 -> 0/27; I-405 32/47 -> 28/47 -> 24/47; SR-520 2/15 -> 1/15 -> 0/15. So 50% fleet penetration relieves most of I-90 and SR-520 congestion but only modestly cuts the worst corridors. (2) Equilibria: yes — a steady state exists at every p (demand < lane supply on most segments; where demand exceeds supply the equilibrium is a congested state at lane capacity, the standard bottleneck equilibrium, not a non-existent state). (3) Tipping points: I-90 p* = 0.73 and SR-520 p* = 0.78 (below these, at least one segment stays at or above capacity; above, none do). I-5 and I-405 have NO tipping point up to p = 0.95 in the base case — 24 and 24 congested segments remain at p = 0.90 — and the 24-combination sweep (f, alpha, g_pen, d all at interval extremes) shows the I-5/I-405 no-tipping result is robust: under no tested combination do they clear by p = 0.95. I-90/SR-520 tipping points move between ~0.2 and 0.9 with f and d. (4) Dedicated lanes: the exchange-3 rule (a dedicated lane must move more people/hour than the general lane it displaces) is not met at p = 0.10 or 0.50 on any corridor (e.g. I-5 at p=0.50: dedicated 1199 vs displaced 2399 people/h); at p = 0.90 it is met only on I-405 (2728 vs 2500 people/h), and still not on I-5 (2159 vs 2399). Conclusion: do not dedicate lanes below ~90% fleet penetration, and then only where fleet demand saturates the lane (I-405's high ADT on 2-3 lanes qualifies; I-5's wide sections do not). Other policy changes suggested by the model: (i) target the two 2-lane I-5 segments near the I-90 junction (mp 163.36-165.29, ADT 236,000-242,000) with a capacity or lane-geometric fix before any AV policy, since no p fixes them; (ii) prioritize managed/AV-lane investment on I-405, the corridor with the highest vphpl (worst 3982) and the only one where a dedicated lane passes the people-throughput test at high p; (iii) because the gain of cooperation is a supply-side one that is diluted by every human in the mix, set a minimum fleet-share threshold (here ~50-75%) before mandating cooperation benefits, and (iv) treat SR-520 as the cheapest corridor to clear (p* = 0.78, short 12.8-mi corridor). Limitations and biases: (i) ADT is a 24-hour total — the 8-12% peak-hour factor is an empirical calibration, and a 25% error in f shifts every tipping point (sweep: I-90 p* ranges 0.2-0.9 over f in [0.08, 0.12]); (ii) the dataset has no directional flow, so d is an assumption — a 10-point change in d changes I-5's congested-segment count at p=0.10 from 42 to 61; (iii) platooning gains were taken at face value from domain estimates and are known to vanish in queueing/low-speed conditions, so the model overstates benefits exactly where congestion is deepest (a built-in optimism bias at the binding constraint); (iv) no induced-demand or route-switching response is modeled, so high-p capacity relief may attract offsetting demand; (v) segment-level lane counts vary within a corridor and the model treats each segment independently (no spillback across segment boundaries); (vi) results are planning-level: they locate where and at what p congestion clears, but the absolute vphpl figures carry the full uncertainty of (i)-(iv), so the defensible outputs are the ordering of corridors, the robust no-tipping result for I-5/I-405, and the relative (not absolute) size of the p=0.50 benefit.
